headline: Global diesel market remains in deficit with inventories drawing; diesel crack spread expected to stay elevated alongside rising crude
reasoning: Gelder noted that global diesel demand continues to exceed global diesel supply from the refining system, so inventories are still drawing. This structural deficit means diesel crack spreads — the premium of diesel over crude — are expected to remain elevated even as crude prices rise. The combination of Hormuz disruption cutting crude availability and Ukrainian strikes reducing Russian refinery throughputs is tightening the refined products market simultaneously from two directions.
quote: Availability will remain tight because if we just think of diesel, global diesel demand is still higher than global diesel supply from the refining system. So inventories continue to draw. So basically what we're expecting is crude prices to continue to rise and diesel's crack spread. So it's premium over crude to remain elevated.

headline: Brent crude seen reaching $100–$105/barrel by year-end if Hormuz remains disrupted; structurally blocked straits could require product prices of $250–$300/barrel to destroy enough demand
reasoning: Wood Mackenzie's base case is dated Brent reaching $100–105/barrel by end of 2025 if the Strait of Hormuz remains in its current standoff configuration. If a peace deal does not materialise in January, crude prices would push higher still. Gelder highlighted that product prices are already at a very high premium over crude; on a normal crude-to-products relationship, current conditions would be equivalent to roughly $150/barrel crude. In a scenario of a significant, structural, long-duration blockade, product prices of $250–$300/barrel would be needed to destroy enough demand to balance the market.
quote: We have a thesis. So it will continue to go higher. The key question is how much flow transits the straits in this stand off type position which we're estimating about 5 to 6,000,000 barrels a day. So we are expecting sort of Brent to dated Brent to get to maybe 100 and 105 dollars a barrel by the end, by the end of the year if the straights and then our assumption or hope is that a peace deal breaks out and flow starts to resume in January. If that is not the case then crude prices will continue to take a little bit higher. The challenge is when people talk about oil price, what's different this time is the very high premium that products are over crude. So if we were to take a normal relationship between crude and products that probably be equivalent now of another price of $150.00 a barrel rather than just under 100. The price at which sort of the world might balance if the straits are blocked significantly and structurally for a long period, product prices would need to be 250 to $300 a barrel.

headline: Alternative Middle East export routes would take many years to build; only increased Hormuz transit or Chinese refinery utilisation can meaningfully relieve near-term supply pressure
reasoning: Gelder dismissed the viability of alternative export infrastructure as a near-term fix, noting these are large, cross-border projects that take many years even after investment decisions are made. The more realistic near-term relief valve is greater flow through the Straits, which would allow Chinese refineries to run harder and export more products, reducing the crack spread. US refining is already running flat out and US crude production growth is only modest.
quote: The issue around sort of egress for the Middle East countries is if they're looking for alternative export routes, those are large complicated infrastructure projects with a number of crossing borders, which means actually they will, even if their investment decisions are taken quickly, they're large projects and they'll take many years to develop. So the only way that this pressure gets relieved is more flows — one is more flows to the straits so that countries in Asia, say particularly China is comfortable. There's plenty of crude available, in which case they will allow their refineries to run harder to export more and that will reduce the premium of products over crude.

headline: Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries are a second major tightening factor for global product markets, alongside Hormuz; resolution of both conflicts needed to normalise prices
reasoning: Gelder emphasised that Ukrainian military strikes have been effective at reducing throughput at Russian refineries, which were historically large exporters of refined products. Their reduced availability is an additional tightening force in the global products market. A normalisation of global oil prices therefore requires resolution of both the Iran-US Hormuz standoff and the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
quote: The other thing that's contributing to this is the Ukrainians have been very effective at hitting and slowing reducing throughputs at Russian refineries and Russian refiners. Traditionally we're a big, we're a big exporter of products. Their lack of availability is also tightening the market. So it's effectively a resolution of those two conflicts is what we need to see for us to get back to a more normal oil price environment.
episode_title: Alan sees oil at $105 if Hormuz stays shut

headline: Asia's crude import dependence rising to 82% by 2030 as regional demand grows and domestic production falls; Middle East and Russia supply disruptions structurally redirect Asian sourcing toward more distant US and Americas barrels
reasoning: Wood Mackenzie projects that Asia's share of crude supplied by imports will reach 82% by 2030, driven by growing oil demand concentrated in Asia while upstream production in the region declines. Refineries in Asia will increasingly need crude from more distant sources. Russia and the Middle East, the traditional nearby suppliers, face structural constraints. The Americas, particularly the US, are growing sources but are geographically distant, adding freight and logistics complexity.
quote: Demand, oil demand is growing globally, but predominantly in Asia, oil production actually is in decline. And so what we're seeing is as the refining, as time moves on, there'll be more and more refineries in Asia, they'll need more crude. That crude will need to come from increasingly further distances. So it's a reflection of the disparity between where crude is produced and where the products are, where product demand is and where the refining system is. So it's sort of a feature of upstream geology and the fact that in a sense where crude is produced in significant volumes, Russia, Middle East, there are restrictions. The other is the US and the Americas. They'd be growing sources of crude, but they're a long way from Asia, hence the need for a greater proportion of their crude coming from imports.

headline: Strait of Hormuz disruption restricting ~5–6 million barrels/day of flow; extended blockade to year-end seen cutting global crude runs by 1.4 million barrels/day in Q4
reasoning: Alan Gelder estimates the current double blockade by Iran and the US Navy is relatively porous but still restricting around 5–6 million barrels per day. Wood Mackenzie had hoped the Strait would open in September but now expects no resumption before January next year. This constrains refining runs and crude availability, keeping product prices high and potentially pushing them higher. The global oil market is already undersupplied, so any further restriction compounds the pressure.
quote: There's certainly a restriction that's of the order of 5 to 6,000,000 barrels a day, we understand right now. So the old market is still undersupplied. And would it? Mackenzie estimating that an extension of the conflict to the end of the year could reduce global crude runs by 1.4 million barrels a day in the fourth quarter.
